objectives: Reason about Ih ice physics + thermodynamics.
Apply Glen's flow law to glacier creep.

slides.title: The cryosphere: Earth's frozen domain
slides.body:
**Cryosphere** (from Greek *kryos* = cold): all the frozen-water components of the Earth system. ~10% of Earth's land surface; ~7% of the ocean (seasonal); contains ~70% of all freshwater on the planet (almost all of it locked in Greenland + Antarctica).

**Components**:
- **Glaciers + small ice caps**: ~200,000 glaciers globally; ~0.5% of Earth's land. Total volume ~158,000 km³ ice-equivalent (~0.4 m sea-level equivalent SLE). Found in High Mountain Asia (Karakoram, Himalaya, Tibet, HKH), Andes, Alps, Rockies, Alaska, Patagonia, New Zealand Southern Alps, Scandinavia, Iceland, Caucasus, East African mountains.
- **Greenland Ice Sheet (GrIS)**: ~1.7 million km² area; ~2.9 million km³ volume; ~7.4 m SLE. ~3000 m thick at center.
- **Antarctic Ice Sheet (AIS)**: ~14 million km² area; ~26.5 million km³ volume; ~58 m SLE. Two main parts — East Antarctic Ice Sheet (EAIS, stable, on bedrock above sea level) + West Antarctic Ice Sheet (WAIS, marine-based, vulnerable to Marine Ice Sheet Instability). Antarctic Peninsula.
- **Sea ice**: floating ice on polar oceans. Arctic ~15 M km² winter / ~4-5 M km² summer (declining ~13% per decade since 1979). Antarctic ~18 M km² winter / ~2-3 M km² summer (more variable).
- **Ice shelves**: floating extensions of grounded ice sheets. Ross + Ronne-Filchner in Antarctica (each ~500,000 km²); Petermann + 79N in Greenland.
- **Permafrost**: ground frozen ≥2 consecutive years. ~24% of Northern Hemisphere land (~15 M km²). Continuous (>90% area), discontinuous, sporadic. Active layer thaws each summer.
- **Seasonal snow**: ~46 M km² peak winter NH; ~26 M km² peak SH. Albedo + hydrology importance.
- **Lake + river ice**, **subglacial ice**, **alpine periglacial features**.

**Role in the climate system**:
- **Albedo**: snow + ice ~0.5-0.9 vs ocean ~0.06 + land ~0.1-0.3. Ice-albedo feedback amplifies polar warming.
- **Heat capacity buffer**: phase-change latent heat (334 kJ/kg fusion) buffers seasonal cycle.
- **Sea level**: GrIS + AIS contain ~65 m SLE; current global mean sea-level rise ~3.6 mm/yr (2006-2018; IPCC AR6) with cryosphere contributing ~half + accelerating.
- **Ocean circulation**: deep-water formation in Nordic Seas + Weddell + Ross Seas drives the global thermohaline circulation (MOC). Sea-ice + glacial-meltwater fluxes matter.
- **Carbon storage**: permafrost holds ~1500 Gt C (~2× atmospheric C); thaw is a major climate feedback.
- **Freshwater supply**: ~1.9 billion people downstream of glacier-fed rivers; HKH 'Asian water tower' supplies Indus, Ganges, Brahmaputra, Yangtze, Yellow, Mekong.

**Why study glaciology now**: cryosphere is the *most-rapidly-changing* component of the climate system. Arctic warming 2-4× global mean. AR6 (Fox-Kemper + Hugelius + Hock + Slater chapter authors) is the strongest IPCC statement on cryospheric change to date.

slides.title: Ice physics: Ih, phase diagram, density
slides.body:
**Crystallography**: at terrestrial pressures + temperatures, water freezes into **ice Ih** (hexagonal). Oxygens occupy a tetrahedral wurtzite-like lattice; hydrogens form a disordered network of H-bonds (Bernal-Fowler ice rules: each O has 2 covalent + 2 H-bonded H neighbors). Hexagonal symmetry gives snowflakes their six-fold habit (Nakaya diagram of crystal habits vs T + supersaturation).

**Other ice polymorphs**: under high pressure, water freezes into ice II, III, V, VI, VII, VIII, IX, ... (~20 known phases). In glaciers + ice sheets pressures rarely exceed ~30 MPa (3000 m ice column), so Ih dominates. Ice VII + X exist deep in icy moons (Europa, Ganymede) + exoplanets.

**Phase diagram**:
- Triple point at 273.16 K (0.01 °C), 611 Pa.
- Atmospheric-pressure freezing point: 273.15 K (0 °C). Famously decreases slightly with pressure (~0.0074 K/atm) — the **Clausius-Clapeyron slope is negative** for water because ice is less dense than liquid (one of water's anomalies). This pressure-melting effect contributes to **basal melting + sliding** of glaciers + ice streams (typically a few tenths of °C beneath thick ice).
- Solid-vapor sublimation curve relevant in cold deserts + ice-shelf surface.

**Density**:
- Pure ice Ih at 0 °C: **917 kg/m³** (less dense than water at 999.8 kg/m³ — ice floats).
- Freshly fallen snow: ~50-200 kg/m³.
- Old firn: ~400-830 kg/m³ (firn = compacted multi-year snow not yet ice).
- **Firn-to-ice transition (close-off depth)**: ~830 kg/m³; air bubbles seal off; depth typically ~50-100 m (Greenland) to ~100-120 m (Antarctica). Critical for ice-core gas-age determination.
- Pure ice density slightly *decreases* with rising T (anomalous; thermal expansion).

**Impurities + composition**:
- Dissolved gases (mostly N₂, O₂) form trapped bubbles below close-off → paleoatmosphere archive.
- **Stable isotopes**: H₂¹⁶O vs HD¹⁶O vs H₂¹⁸O fractionate during evaporation + condensation (Rayleigh distillation). δ¹⁸O + δD are temperature proxies — Dansgaard 1964 calibrated δ¹⁸O ≈ 0.69 T_avg − 13.6 ‰ for Greenland.
- **Dust + ash + sea salt + black carbon**: aerosol record; Saharan dust layers, volcanic tephra, biomass-burning soot.
- **Cosmogenic radionuclides**: ¹⁰Be, ³⁶Cl, ¹⁴C for dating + solar-activity reconstruction.

**Mechanical properties** (relevant for flow):
- Young's modulus ~9 GPa.
- Brittle at fast strain rates (cracks, crevasses); ductile at slow rates (creep).
- Anisotropic — basal plane (perpendicular to c-axis) is the easy-glide plane, ~60× softer than the prism + pyramidal planes. Ice fabric (crystal-orientation distribution) develops with deformation history — modeled via fabric tensor + observed in ice cores.
- **Thermal conductivity** ~2.1 W/(m·K) at 0 °C, increasing as T drops. Cold ice diffuses heat slowly → ice sheet thermal inertia ~10⁵ yr.

slides.title: Ice rheology: Glen's flow law + creep
slides.body:
Glaciers + ice sheets *flow* — slowly. They are non-Newtonian fluids: viscosity depends nonlinearly on stress. The constitutive equation is **Glen's flow law** (Glen 1955; refined by Nye 1953 + 1957, Steinemann 1958, Paterson 1994):

  ε̇ = A τ^n

where ε̇ is strain rate, τ is effective deviatoric stress, **n ≈ 3** (typical 2.5-4), and **A** is a temperature-dependent rate factor following an Arrhenius relation:

  A(T) = A₀ exp(−Q / (R T))

Activation energy Q ≈ 60 kJ/mol below −10 °C, ≈ 140 kJ/mol above (transition due to grain-boundary + premelting effects). A roughly doubles per 10 °C warming below −10 °C → warmer ice flows dramatically faster.

**John Nye** (Bristol, 1953-1965) developed the theoretical framework: derived the parallel-sided-slab solution + the surface-slope-driven flow, founding modern theoretical glaciology. **Charles Raymond + Garry Clarke + Ian Joughin + Eric Rignot + Hilmar Gudmundsson** built on it.

**Glen-law consequences for a parallel-sided slab on a slope α**:
- Driving stress: τ_d = ρ g h sin α (typical 50-150 kPa for valley glaciers).
- Surface velocity (deformation only): u_s = (2 A / (n+1)) (ρ g sin α)^n h^(n+1).
- For n = 3: **u_s ∝ h⁴ × (sin α)³** — thicker + steeper glaciers flow vastly faster.

**Creep mechanisms** (microscale):
- **Dislocation creep** (basal slip): primary mode; basal plane slips easily.
- **Diffusional creep** (Nabarro-Herring, Coble): dominant at low stress + high T.
- **Grain-boundary sliding**: contributes at fine grain size.
- **Recrystallization**: fabric evolution under stress.

**Beyond Glen**:
- **Anisotropy**: oriented fabric softens or stiffens depending on stress direction; ~10× effect in extreme fabrics. Models (CAFFE, ELLE-FEVOR).
- **Damage mechanics**: micro-cracks pre-failure (especially shear margins, ice-shelf flexure, calving fronts).
- **Hydrology coupling**: liquid water at grain boundaries weakens ice.
- **Impurity effects**: dust + soluble ions modulate A.

**Sliding vs deformation**:
- **Internal deformation** (Glen flow): cold, frozen-bed glaciers (most of Antarctica). Velocities m/yr to tens of m/yr.
- **Basal sliding**: where bed is at pressure-melting point; meltwater lubricates. Can dominate motion (~90% of surface velocity for fast ice streams + outlet glaciers). Velocities ~100-10000 m/yr (Jakobshavn ~17 km/yr).
- **Ice-stream flow**: Bindschadler + Whillans named WAIS ice streams; sliding-dominated, characterized by Shelfy-Stream Approximation (SSA, see next lesson).

**Bridging stresses**: in shear margins, ice-shelf flexure, near grounding lines, non-Glen behavior arises + must be treated via full-Stokes models (Elmer/Ice, ISSM, BISICLES).

**Connection to ice-core analysis**: knowledge of A(T) is what lets us back out flow histories from observed deformation; ice-core fabric measurements calibrate microphysical models. The whole chain — from molecular ice physics through grain-scale rheology to ice-sheet flow — is the foundation of modern glaciology.

question.question: Compute the surface velocity of a parallel-sided glacier slab
question.goal: A temperate-glacier slab is 200 m thick, slope α = 5°, T = −2 °C (so A ≈ 6.8×10⁻²⁴ Pa⁻³ s⁻¹). Use ρ = 917 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s², n = 3. Compute driving stress + surface velocity.

steps.prompt: Driving stress τ_d = ρ g h sin α. Compute (kPa).
steps.reveal: τ_d = 917 × 9.81 × 200 × sin(5°) ≈ 917 × 9.81 × 200 × 0.0872 ≈ 1.57×10⁵ Pa ≈ 157 kPa. Typical valley-glacier driving stress (50-150 kPa range; this is at the high end).

steps.prompt: Glen-law surface velocity u_s = (2 A / (n+1)) τ_d^n h. Compute (m/yr). 1 yr ≈ 3.15×10⁷ s.
steps.reveal: u_s = (2 × 6.8×10⁻²⁴ / 4) × (1.57×10⁵)³ × 200 = 3.4×10⁻²⁴ × 3.87×10¹⁵ × 200 = 2.6×10⁻⁶ m/s ≈ 83 m/yr. (Sensitive to A — small changes in T or fabric easily move this by factor 2-3.) Real Alpine valley glaciers move ~10-100 m/yr; consistent.

steps.prompt: If T dropped to −20 °C (so A ≈ 1.0×10⁻²⁴), by what factor does u_s change?
hints: A scales velocity linearly; new A is ~6.8× smaller.
steps.reveal: u_s ∝ A → A drops by factor 6.8 → velocity drops by factor 6.8. This is why cold (East Antarctic) ice flows ~10-100× slower than temperate (Alpine, GrIS coastal) ice for the same geometry — the Arrhenius A(T) dominance. Glen's law + thermal regime together explain the polar/temperate flow contrast.

steps.prompt: If basal sliding contributes equal motion, what's total surface speed?
steps.reveal: u_total = u_deform + u_slide = 83 + 83 ≈ 166 m/yr. Sliding is the dominant additional control for fast ice — Pine Island, Jakobshavn, Thwaites, Whillans ice stream all sliding-dominated. Inferring sliding from observed velocity requires modeled deformation as residual (inversion via Joughin + Rignot + Gudmundsson methods).

question.question: Why is the cryosphere often called the 'most rapidly changing' component of the Earth system?
options: Cryosphere change is amplified relative to global mean because of multiple positive feedbacks: ice-albedo (loss of bright ice → more absorption → more warming → more loss); lapse-rate feedback in the Arctic (more surface trapping); ice-thickness feedback (thinner ice melts faster); ocean stratification under melt. Result: Arctic warming 2-4× global mean (Arctic amplification); summer Arctic sea ice declined ~50% since 1979 (PIOMAS volume; satellite extent); Greenland + Antarctica mass-loss accelerating (GRACE, IMBIE 2020); permafrost thaw widening + deepening; alpine glaciers lost ~50% volume over the 20th century. IPCC AR6 (Hock + Slater + Stocker + Fox-Kemper chapter authors) treats the cryosphere as the system component furthest from quasi-equilibrium — most likely to cross tipping points + with the strongest committed change.
question.explanation: Cryosphere amplification: ice-albedo, lapse-rate, ice-thickness feedbacks → Arctic warms 2-4× global mean. Summer Arctic sea ice ~50% reduced since 1979; Greenland + Antarctica mass loss accelerating; permafrost thaw widespread; alpine glaciers ~50% volume loss in 20th century. IPCC AR6 emphasizes the cryosphere as the most-rapidly-changing system component + most likely to cross tipping points.

slides.workedSolution: Multiple positive feedbacks (ice-albedo, lapse-rate, ice-thickness) → Arctic amplification. Summer Arctic sea ice halved since 1979; Greenland + Antarctica losing mass at accelerating rate; permafrost thaw deepening; alpine glaciers ~50% lost in 20th century. AR6 treats cryosphere as most rapidly changing + most tipping-prone component.

question.question: A new ice-core site
question.prompt: A drilling program plans to extract an ice core at a site in East Antarctica where snow accumulation is 30 kg/m²/yr + ice thickness is 3500 m. Estimate the age range achievable + describe what physical + chemical signals you would prioritize measuring + why.

question.question: If Glen-law n = 3 + ice thickness doubles, by what factor does the slab-flow surface velocity increase (all else equal)?
question.hint: u_s ∝ h^(n+1) = h⁴; doubling h gives 2⁴ = 16.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why understanding ice rheology (Glen's flow law + Arrhenius temperature dependence) is foundational for projecting future sea-level rise from Greenland + Antarctica.
question.rubric: Mentions: Glen's flow law ε̇ = A τ^n (Glen 1955, Nye 1953) with n ≈ 3 means ice flow is highly nonlinear in stress — small geometric changes (steeper, thicker) produce large velocity changes (u ∝ h⁴ sin³ α for slab). A(T) Arrhenius with Q ~60-140 kJ/mol means a ~10 °C warming roughly doubles A → warmer ice flows much faster. Combined with basal-sliding regimes, fabric anisotropy + damage, rheology controls the speed at which marine ice sheets respond to ocean + atmospheric forcing. Future projections (ISMIP6 ensembles, AR6 chapter authors Slater + Edwards + DeConto + Pollard) hinge on properly representing flow physics. Why it matters: Greenland holds 7.4 m sea-level equivalent + Antarctica 58 m; getting timescales right (centuries vs millennia) depends on Glen rheology + the sliding + calving + grounding-line physics layered on top. Without solid rheology, future sea-level uncertainties remain unbounded.
